planting.note: Plant shallow rhizome divisions just below the soil surface in late summer or early fall into slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; do not bury the rhizome deeply or it will rot.

directions: This pure-white sport of the native dwarf crested iris carries the same crested falls and gold-and-white throat markings as the species, but entirely without the typical lavender-blue pigment, making it glow in shaded borders at dusk. Plant shallow rhizomes just below the soil surface in humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade, where it will spread by branching surface rhizomes to form a dense flowering carpet within two to three seasons. It blooms in early to mid-spring alongside the species form and pairs beautifully with the blue-flowered wild type or with early ephemerals like bloodroot and trillium. Divide congested colonies immediately after flowering, replanting divisions right away since exposed rhizomes dry out quickly.

planting.note: Plant shallow rhizome divisions just below the soil surface in late summer or early fall into slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; this Eco-Gardens selection spreads readily once established.

directions: Selected and introduced by Don Jacobs of Eco-Gardens in Georgia, this dwarf crested iris cultivar bears richly saturated deep blue-violet flowers with a bold white-and-gold crest, a shade or two darker than typical wild colonies. Plant shallow rhizomes just below the soil surface in humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade under deciduous trees or along shaded rock outcrops, where established plantings spread quickly into a dense, weed-suppressing carpet. Bloom occurs in early to mid-spring for two to three weeks before the tree canopy fully closes. Divide crowded clumps in late summer if flowering declines, keeping divisions moist until replanted since the shallow rhizomes dry out and die quickly once exposed to air.

planting.note: Plant shallow rhizome divisions just below the soil surface in late summer or early fall into slightly acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade; do not plant deeply.

directions: Named for the North Carolina mountain slope where it was originally collected, this dwarf crested iris selection is prized for its striking pale blue-and-white falls overlaid with a fine network of darker violet veining, more pronounced than the typical wild form. Plant shallow surface rhizomes in humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade under deciduous trees, where colonies spread steadily to form a dense flowering groundcover. It flowers in early to mid-spring for two to three weeks, then persists as attractive low fan-shaped foliage through summer before going semi-dormant. Divide congested colonies right after bloom, replanting divisions immediately since the shallow rhizomes desiccate quickly once lifted.

common_name: Smooth Dwarf Violet Iris (Small's Dwarf Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in well-drained, acidic, sandy to loamy soil in partial shade to full sun; this Coastal Plain and Piedmont variety tolerates less-perfectly-drained soil than the mountain-form var. verna.

directions: This robust coastal and piedmont variety of dwarf violet iris grows taller and spreads more vigorously than the mountain-form typical variety, with slightly larger violet-blue, yellow-signaled flowers held on stems to 6-8 inches. Plant rhizome divisions in fall in acidic, well-drained sandy or loamy soil in partial shade to full sun, mimicking the open pine woodland and sandhill habitats of the Southeastern Coastal Plain where it naturally occurs. It blooms in early spring, among the earliest native irises to flower, and slowly forms a low spreading colony via narrow rhizomes. Best used naturalized in acidic sandhill or pine-woodland gardens; avoid heavy clay or poorly drained sites, which quickly rot the rhizomes.
